title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization global ticketId binding enables relayer-ordering censorship of pre-approved commits
root_cause: The authorization object is bound to an exact `ticketId`, while `ticketId` is a single global queue (`commitments.length`) that can change between approval and execution. Because only `RelayerEscrow.owner()` can execute `commitOnBehalf`, the relayer fully controls sequencing and can invalidate previously approved authorizations by inserting other commits first.
trigger_scenario: Two users obtain backend-signed commit authorizations that both target the current next ticket id.
Both users call `approveCommitAuthorization`, storing hashes that include that specific ticket id.
Relayer owner executes one commit first via `commitOnBehalf`, incrementing `commitments.length` in `RevealMarket`.
The second user's authorized payload now fails `auth.ticketId == commitments.length` in `commitWithAuthorization` with `TicketIndexMismatch`.
By repeatedly choosing ordering (or withholding execution) the relayer can force selected users to re-sign/re-approve until the commit window closes.
preconditions: Commit execution is centralized through `RelayerEscrow.commitOnBehalf` (`onlyOwner`).
Authorizations are pre-signed for a concrete `ticketId` before on-chain execution.
There is contention or intentional ordering manipulation before `commitDeadline`.

title: RelayerEscrow.approveCommitAuthorization creates non-revocable approvals that relayer owner can execute at arbitrary later times
root_cause: Approved commit authorizations are stored as a persistent boolean and there is no user-side revoke/cancel path. Execution timing is entirely delegated to `onlyOwner` `commitOnBehalf`, so approvals stay live until consumed (or naturally expired in market checks), even if user intent changes.
trigger_scenario: User approves a commit authorization with a long `expiry` via `approveCommitAuthorization`.
Relayer does not execute immediately and the approval remains `true` in `approvedCommitAuthorizations`.
User later changes intent but cannot revoke that authorization on-chain.
At any later point before expiry, relayer owner executes `commitOnBehalf` once user balance is sufficient.
User is forced into a commitment at relayer-chosen timing without a fresh consent transaction.
preconditions: A valid approval exists for `(user, authHash)` and has not been consumed.
`auth.expiry` has not elapsed when execution is attempted.
Relayer owner behaves adversarially or is compromised.

title: RelayerEscrow._safeTransferExact and RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization trust token-reported balances, enabling phantom collateral if token is adversarial
root_cause: Collateral movement and backing checks are validated only via `IERC20.balanceOf` deltas from the same external token contract being checked. If the token is upgradeable/non-standard and can lie about balances, `_safeTransferExact` and market backing predicates can be satisfied without an economically equivalent transfer.
trigger_scenario: Collateral token implementation is upgraded or deployed with adversarial `balanceOf` semantics.
`commitOnBehalf` calls `_safeTransferExact`, and token reports sender/recipient deltas consistent with an exact transfer even when real spendable balances did not move equivalently.
`commitWithAuthorization` passes `balanceOf(address(this)) >= totalEscrow + ticketSize` using the same manipulated view.
Escrow debits user accounting and market records commitment/rake based on assumed payment.
At settlement/claim time, liabilities are under-backed in real token terms, leading to insolvency or payout failure.
preconditions: Collateral token is non-standard, malicious, or mutable (e.g., upgradeable) and can return deceptive balances.
Protocol relies exclusively on token-reported balances for transfer correctness and payment backing.
Commits continue under this token behavior before detection.

title: RevealMarket.extendCommitDeadline: Missing expiry guard allows reopening commits after deadline, enabling late-position insertion before lock
root_cause: extendCommitDeadline() only checks monotonic increase and one-shot/max-range constraints, but never requires block.timestamp <= commitDeadline. Because commitWithAuthorization() gates on the mutable commitDeadline value, a factory owner can extend after the original deadline has already passed and reopen the commit window.
trigger_scenario: Users submit commitments until the original commitDeadline and stop because commit window appears closed.
Original deadline passes, but oracle has not yet called lockBatches().
Factory owner calls extendMarketCommitDeadline(), which forwards to RevealMarket.extendCommitDeadline() and sets a new future deadline without checking that the previous deadline already expired.
Relayer resumes commitWithAuthorization() calls because block.timestamp is now below the new commitDeadline.
Oracle can no longer lock immediately since lockBatches() now requires waiting for the extended deadline.
Late commitments are inserted with more information than earlier participants had, breaking market fairness and deadline finality assumptions.
preconditions: Market is still in Phase.Commit (not yet locked).
Original commit deadline has elapsed, and factory owner is willing to extend once.
Relayer continues accepting commits after extension.

evidence.snippet: extendCommitDeadline checks only newDeadline>commitDeadline, phase==Commit, one-shot flag, and max extension; no check that block.timestamp is still before current commitDeadline.
commitWithAuthorization allows commits whenever block.timestamp < commitDeadline, so extending commitDeadline re-opens commit acceptance.
lockBatches requires block.timestamp >= commitDeadline, so extension also delays locking and finalization.
Factory owner can invoke extendMarketCommitDeadline at any time while market remains in commit phase.

title: RevealMarket.enableRefunds: Timeout cancel path can discard posted results and accepted batch proofs, allowing privileged settlement rollback
root_cause: enableRefunds() allows transition from Locked -> Cancelled solely on timeout, without checking resultPosted status or settledBatchCount progress. This lets a privileged factory caller void a market after outcome publication and partial proof acceptance, effectively overriding in-flight settlement state.
trigger_scenario: Market is locked and oracle posts the winning outcome via postResult().
Oracle submits one or more valid batch proofs through verifyAndSettleBatched(), so settledBatchCount and settled sums become non-zero, but not all batches are completed yet.
No final _finalizeSettlement() occurs before lockedAt + SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS.
Factory owner calls enableMarketRefunds(), which forwards to enableRefunds() and flips phase to Cancelled without inspecting resultPosted or partial settlement progress.
All claim paths are disabled by phase check (requires Settled), and only refund paths remain.
Users who should have asymmetric winner payouts are instead forced into symmetric ticket refunds, rolling back economic finality after result revelation.
preconditions: Phase is Locked and settlement timeout has elapsed.
Factory owner can call enableMarketRefunds().
Settlement is partially complete (or at least result is posted) but not finalized.

evidence.snippet: enableRefunds in Locked phase checks only timeout and then sets phase=Cancelled; it does not inspect resultPosted, settledBatchCount, or any settlement-progress fields.
postResult persists outcome (resultPosted=true), but cancellation path does not require this to be false.
_verifyBatchProof records partial progress (settledBatchCount and sums), which can still be abandoned by later enableRefunds timeout cancellation.

title: RevealMarket._safeTransferExact: Strict balance-delta accounting can permanently DoS settlement/claims/refunds when collateral token behavior drifts
root_cause: All payout paths hard-revert unless sender and recipient balance deltas are exactly compatible with a no-fee, non-rebasing token. _safeTransferExact() enforces senderDebited == amount and recipientReceived >= amount using pre/post balanceOf checks. If token mechanics change post-deployment (fee-on-transfer toggle, blacklist side effects, rebasing quirks), claims/refunds/sweeps and even surplus forwarding during finalization can revert indefinitely.
trigger_scenario: Users commit funds and market reaches Locked or Settled lifecycle stages.
Collateral token behavior changes after deployment (e.g., transfer fee activation, blacklist semantics, unusual balance accounting).
Market executes _safeTransferExact() in _finalizeSettlement(), claim(), refund*(), or sweep*().
Pre/post balance checks fail strict invariants (senderDebited != amount or recipientReceived < amount).
Transaction reverts with FeeOnTransferNotSupported.
Because all outbound value paths share this helper, users can be stuck unable to claim or refund, and factory sweep fallback can also fail.
preconditions: Collateral token does not maintain strict no-fee/no-rebase semantics for the full market lifetime.
Market reaches a state requiring token outflow (settle, claim, refund, or sweep).

evidence.snippet: _safeTransferExact requires senderDebited == amount and recipientReceived >= amount based on balanceOf deltas; otherwise it reverts FeeOnTransferNotSupported.
_finalizeSettlement forwards surplus via _safeTransferExact(protocolPool, surplus), so finalization can fail on token semantic drift.
Claims, refunds, and sweep paths all rely on _safeTransferExact, expanding any token-compatibility failure into a full lifecycle payout DoS.

title: RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash: Locked verifier anchor is non-recoverable, so key drift hard-locks settlement until cancellation
root_cause: lockBatches snapshots lockedVerifierKeyHash once, and both verify paths require exact equality forever. The so-called refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash() path only re-checks equality and emits an event; it never updates the stored anchor. If verifier key hash drifts for operational reasons, market settlement becomes unrecoverable in Locked phase and can only exit via timeout cancellation.
trigger_scenario: Market is locked and stores lockedVerifierKeyHash from current verifier.
Verifier key hash changes later (e.g., emergency rotation, verifier redeploy policy mismatch, or ownership/governance maintenance event).
verifyAndSettle()/verifyAndSettleBatched() revert due VerifierNotApproved or VerifierKeyMismatch checks.
Factory attempts refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey(), but market.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash() enforces current key == lockedVerifierKeyHash and does not write new state.
Settlement cannot progress even before any batch proof is accepted.
After timeout, only cancellation/refund path remains, sacrificing intended settlement finality.
preconditions: Phase is Locked with unsettled batches.
Verifier key hash no longer matches lockedVerifierKeyHash.
Factory cannot or does not finalize before timeout.

evidence.snippet: Locked key hash is captured once at lock and enforced by both settlement entry points.
refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash checks equality and emits an event, but never updates lockedVerifierKeyHash.
Factory refresh helper delegates to the no-op refresh path; there is no alternate state transition to rotate locked key anchor.

title: MarketFactory.setVerifierApproval + RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash pin verifier keys in a way that can deadlock locked markets after verifier key rotation
root_cause: Factory governance permanently pins `approvedVerifierKeyHash` per verifier address, while `Verifier` allows owner key rotation. Once a market is locked, `refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey` does not actually write a new key hash (it only re-checks equality) and `setVerifier` is unavailable outside Commit phase, so a post-lock verifier key rotation creates an unrecoverable policy mismatch.
trigger_scenario: A market enters `Phase.Locked` and stores `lockedVerifierKeyHash` during `lockBatches`.
The verifier owner rotates the proving key via `Verifier.setVerifyingKey`, changing `verifyingKeyHash` without changing verifier address.
`MarketFactory.isVerifierCurrentlyApproved` starts returning false because on-chain key hash no longer matches pinned `approvedVerifierKeyHash`.

`MarketFactory.refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey` cannot repair the lock because `_validateVerifier` now fails on drift and `RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash` requires equality instead of updating state.
Settlement entrypoints (`verifyAndSettle` / `verifyAndSettleBatched`) fail verifier approval/key checks, leaving market stuck in Locked until timeout-driven refunds.
preconditions: A locked market still needs settlement proofs.
Verifier key material is changed after market lock (maliciously or operationally).
Market cannot be moved back to Commit phase to rotate verifier address.

evidence.snippet: Pins verifier key hash per address and re-approval reverts on drift.
Checks current key equals locked key but never writes a new locked key hash.

title: MarketFactory.setRelayerCommitsPaused is fail-open: pause fanout errors are swallowed so active relayers can remain live during emergency stop
root_cause: Emergency pause propagation uses nested `try/catch` and never reverts on failure; it only emits `RelayerPausePropagationFailed`. The outer function still emits global pause success even if one or more active relayers reject or ignore the pause call.
trigger_scenario: At least one market points to an active relayer in `activeRelayers`.
That relayer reverts or behaves non-standardly when `setCommitsPaused(true)` is called.
Owner invokes `setRelayerCommitsPaused(true)` expecting a protocol-wide commit stop.
`_setRelayerCommitsPausedBatch` catches the failure and continues without reverting the transaction.
The transaction emits pause events, but the failing relayer stays unpaused and can continue forwarding commits for its markets.
preconditions: An active relayer contract can fail/ignore pause updates (misconfiguration, upgrade drift, or malicious relayer implementation).
Operators rely on factory-level pause fanout as an emergency circuit breaker.

evidence.snippet: Pause propagation failures emit events but do not revert.
Global pause event is emitted after best-effort fanout, regardless of per-relayer failures.

title: MarketFactory.migrateMarketRelayerBalances migrates global user escrow balances (not market-scoped), enabling cross-market collateral misrouting
root_cause: Relayer balances are stored per-user globally in `RelayerEscrow` (no market dimension), but `migrateMarketRelayerBalances` is invoked per market and moves `oldRelayer.balances(user)` in full. This couples one market's relayer migration to all of a user's collateral parked on the old relayer.
trigger_scenario: A user keeps collateral on an old relayer for multiple markets.
Factory owner rotates a single market to a new relayer and calls `migrateMarketRelayerBalances` for that market.
The function reads `oldRelayer.balances(user)` and withdraws the full amount, then credits it on the target relayer.
Other markets still tied to the old relayer lose access to that user's previously available escrow balance.
Commits for those markets fail until users manually rebalance collateral across relayers.
preconditions: A user balance on old relayer is intended to serve more than one market.
Factory performs per-market relayer migration using the provided helper.

evidence.snippet: Migrates `oldRelayer.balances(user)` (entire user balance) per user during a single-market migration.
Escrow accounting is `mapping(address => uint256)` without market-level partitioning.

title: RelayerEscrow/ProtocolPool assume non-rebasing collateral; supply rebases can violate backing and reservation invariants across contracts
root_cause: Cross-contract accounting is done in raw token amounts (`balances`, `accountedCollateral`, `reservedTotal`, `reservedLiability`) with no share-based normalization and no token capability gate beyond fee-on-transfer checks. If collateral token balances change asynchronously (negative/positive rebasing), internal accounting can diverge from actual transferable balance.
trigger_scenario: Protocol deploys with an ERC20 that can rebase balances without transfers.
Users deposit into relayer escrow and markets reserve pool liability under pre-rebase balances.
A negative rebase reduces actual token balances in escrow/pool while `balances`, `accountedCollateral`, and reservation state remain unchanged.
Escrow withdraw/commit transfers and pool draw/withdraw checks begin reverting due insufficient real balance relative to accounting expectations.
Users/markets face withdrawal and settlement DoS until external recapitalization occurs.
preconditions: Collateral token supports asynchronous supply/balance rebasing or similar non-standard balance mutation.
Protocol does not hard-restrict collateral to strictly non-rebasing ERC20 implementations.

evidence.snippet: Excess is computed from `balanceOf - accountedCollateral` with no share/rebase adaptation.
Reservations rely on instantaneous `balanceOf` and `reservedTotal` invariants in raw token units.

title: Factory routing rotations are non-atomic across dependencies, leaving stale `allowedMarket` permissions and cross-contract authorization drift
root_cause: Dependency rotations only apply forward registration on the new endpoint, while old endpoint cleanup is missing (`updateMarketProtocolPool`) or best-effort only (`updateMarketRelayer` with swallowed unregister failures). This permits stale `allowedMarket` trust edges to outlive factory routing state.
trigger_scenario: A market is deployed and registered in initial relayer/pool allowlists.
Factory rotates the market to new dependencies.
Old relayer unregister can fail without reverting, and old protocol pool is never explicitly de-authorized.
Factory/market now reference new dependencies, but old dependencies still retain market-level authorization flags.
Subsequent operational rollbacks, misrouting, or unexpected call paths can exercise stale permissions that operators assume were revoked.
preconditions: At least one dependency rotation occurs for an existing market.
Operators assume de-registration is strict and atomic across all protocol-owned dependencies.

evidence.snippet: Old relayer unregister failures are caught and rotation continues.
New pool registration occurs with no corresponding old pool de-registration path.

title: BaseLpVault.withdraw rounds share burn down, allowing over-withdrawal that dilutes other LPs
root_cause: `withdraw()` computes shares to burn via `convertToShares(assets)`, and `convertToShares` uses `Math.mulDiv(... )` with floor rounding. For exact-asset withdrawals, rounding down under-burns shares whenever `assets * totalSupply / totalAssets` is non-integer; ERC4626-style safety requires rounding up for withdraw paths.
trigger_scenario: Vault has non-integer price-per-share, e.g. `totalAssets=150` and `totalSupply=100` after hedging profit donation.
Attacker owns 50 shares (half of supply).
Attacker repeatedly calls `withdraw(2, attacker, attacker)`.
Each call burns `floor(2*100/150)=1` share but transfers 2 assets out.
After 50 calls, attacker burns 50 shares and withdraws 100 assets, even though fair value for 50 shares was 75 assets.
The extra 25 assets are transferred from remaining LPs (value extraction via rounding drift).
preconditions: `totalSupply() > 0` and `totalAssets()`/`totalSupply()` yields non-integer conversion for chosen withdrawal amounts.
Attacker can perform multiple withdrawals (or choose a single amount with favorable floor rounding).
Vault has enough `idleAssets()` to satisfy requested withdrawals.

title: BaseLpVault outbound transfers are assumed exact, so non-standard assets can desynchronize accounting and real balances
root_cause: The vault validates exact amounts only on inbound `safeTransferFrom` paths (`deposit`, `repayFromHedge`) but does not enforce exact sender/receiver deltas for outbound `safeTransfer` paths (`withdraw`, `redeem`, `borrowForHedge`). If the configured 6-decimal asset has directional fees/surcharges/burn semantics on outbound transfers, internal accounting (`utilizedAssets`, burned shares) assumes exact movement while token balances realize different movement.
trigger_scenario: Vault is deployed with a 6-decimal token that behaves non-standard on outbound transfers (e.g., sender surcharge or recipient haircut).
LP calls `withdraw`/`redeem` or hedger calls `borrowForHedge`.
Vault updates state as if `amount` moved exactly (burns shares or increments `utilizedAssets`).
Token transfer applies non-standard fee behavior so actual debited/received value differs from `amount`.
Vault accounting diverges from real balances, causing LP underpayment, utilization mismeasurement, or insolvency drift.
preconditions: Configured `ASSET` is not strict vanilla USDC behavior on outbound transfers.
Outbound transfer paths (`withdraw`, `redeem`, or `borrowForHedge`) are exercised.

title: ProtocolPool LP unlock accounting is unbounded per-user, enabling withdrawal liveness failure via deposit-fragmentation
root_cause: Each `deposit()` appends a new `DepositRecord` and records are never compacted/removed. `lpWithdraw`, `unlockedShares`, and `maxRedeemable` iterate the full per-user `_deposits` array. This creates O(n) gas with unbounded n, so sufficiently fragmented deposit history can make redemption paths exceed block gas limits.
trigger_scenario: An LP (or automation acting for the LP) performs a very large number of small deposits over time.
After lock expiry, LP calls `lpWithdraw` to redeem unlocked shares.
`_burnUnlockedShares` scans the entire `_deposits[lp]` array and may run out of gas before completion.
The same O(n) scan affects `maxRedeemable` and `unlockedShares` queries, degrading front-end and keeper operations.
LP funds become practically stuck until transaction gas limits increase or custom off-chain splitting strategy is used.
preconditions: Per-user deposit record count grows large (many fragmented deposits).
User must rely on loop-based withdrawal path over full historical records.

title: HedgeStrategyExecutor executes signed borrows without enforcing minOut/slippage against realized hedge outcome
root_cause: `Order.minOut` is never used for any on-chain condition and `Order.maxSlippageBps` is only compared to a global admin cap, not to any observed execution result. `executeBorrow` only moves funds from vault to receiver, so signed price-protection fields are not cryptographically bound to downstream execution quality.
trigger_scenario: Signer issues a valid order with conservative `minOut` / `maxSlippageBps` expecting slippage protection.
Any caller submits `executeBorrow` with that signature.
Executor validates signature, nonce, deadline, amount, and receiver allowlist, then borrows funds to receiver.
No on-chain check compares downstream hedge fill to `minOut` or realized slippage.
If receiver-side execution is compromised or adverse, vault funds are still borrowed with no protocol-level slippage enforcement.
preconditions: Receiver is allowed and order signature is valid.
Downstream hedge execution happens off-contract (or not at all), outside enforceable checks in `executeBorrow`.

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Oracle-signed payout is not bound to the committed leaf -> compromised oracle can drain all settled liquidity through one owned ticket
root_cause: claimWithOracleAuthorization() verifies only (ticketId, owner, payout, expiry) against an oracle signature and never recomputes the Poseidon commitment leaf or checks Merkle inclusion for the ticket. The only quantitative guard is claimedLiability <= totalLiability, so any oracle-signed payout amount is accepted even if it does not match the ticket's committed (outcome, amount, payout, salt) preimage.
trigger_scenario: Attacker commits at least one ticket in the market (winning or losing).
After settlement, the oracle key is compromised (or malicious oracle operator acts).
Attacker signs/obtains an oracle authorization for their own ticketId with payout equal to the entire remaining totalLiability and a valid expiry.
Attacker calls claimWithOracleAuthorization(ticketId, hugePayout, expiry, sig).
The contract marks the ticket claimed, updates claimedLiability, and transfers hugePayout to that ticket owner because no leaf/proof validation runs on this path.
Subsequent legitimate tickets fail to claim due to OverClaimed or depleted market balance.
preconditions: Oracle signing key is compromised or oracle is malicious.
Attacker controls at least one committed ticket owner address.

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Missing per-ticket nonce/version lets stale low-value signatures be frontrun -> ticket can be permanently underpaid
root_cause: Oracle claim authorizations include payout and expiry but no monotonic nonce/version tracked per ticket. The contract accepts the first valid signature submitted and sets claimedTickets[ticketId] = true, so older signatures remain valid until expiry and cannot be revoked on-chain.
trigger_scenario: Oracle issues a first authorization for ticketId with payout P1 (for example during an initial off-chain calculation).
Oracle later issues a corrected authorization for the same ticket with payout P2 > P1.
Both signatures are observable by third parties (API leak, relayer logs, or mempool exposure).
An attacker submits the stale P1 signature first via claimWithOracleAuthorization.
The contract marks the ticket as claimed and transfers only P1.
The corrected P2 authorization becomes unusable because TicketAlreadyClaimed now blocks all further claims for that ticket.
preconditions: More than one valid oracle authorization exists for the same ticketId.
At least one stale/lower authorization is still unexpired when submitted.

title: RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused/_effectiveClaimDeadline: Ongoing pause time extends claim deadline in real-time -> claims and sweep can be frozen indefinitely
root_cause: When claims are paused in Settled phase, _effectiveClaimDeadline() adds (block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt) continuously. claim() is blocked by claimsPaused, and sweepUnclaimed() requires block.timestamp > _effectiveClaimDeadline(). While paused, effective deadline moves forward with current time, so sweep condition can never become true until an explicit unpause occurs. No max pause duration or emergency sweep bypass exists.
trigger_scenario: Market reaches Settled and claimDeadline is initialized.
Factory owner calls setClaimsPaused(true), setting claimPauseStartedAt = now.
Users cannot call claim because ClaimsPaused reverts.
As time passes, _effectiveClaimDeadline grows by the same amount (now - claimPauseStartedAt), so it stays ahead of block.timestamp.
Factory cannot call sweepUnclaimed because ClaimWindowOpen keeps reverting while paused.
If pause is never lifted (operator failure, key loss, or malicious governance), both user claims and terminal sweeping are permanently blocked.
preconditions: Market is in Settled phase.
Claims are paused and not later unpaused by factory governance.

title: RevealMarket._verifyLeaf path depends on unverified lockBatches roots -> oracle+relayer can make trustless claims impossible and force trusted payout path
root_cause: claim() requires both commitments[ticketId] == leaf and a Merkle proof to batchRoots[batchIndex], but lockBatches() never recomputes/validates roots from on-chain commitments. It only checks counts and a relayer-owner signature over supplied roots. If supplied roots do not correspond to stored commitments, users cannot satisfy _verifyLeaf even with correct preimages.
trigger_scenario: Users commit valid ticket leaves, which are stored in commitments[].
At lock time, oracle submits batch roots that are inconsistent with commitments[] but still passes count checks.
Relayer owner signature is provided (collusion, compromise, or blind signing of incorrect roots).
Settlement completes against those roots.
Winning users call claim with correct (ticketId, outcome, amount, payout, salt) and fail InvalidMerkleProof because no proof can satisfy both commitment equality and mismatched batch root.
Only claimWithOracleAuthorization remains, shifting payout correctness from cryptographic leaf membership to trusted oracle signatures.
preconditions: Oracle submits incorrect batch roots during lock.
Relayer owner signs or is compromised for those roots.

title: RevealMarket claim/refund payout recipient is immutable ticket owner -> blacklist/frozen addresses become unclaimable and are swept to protocol pool
root_cause: All payout paths transfer only to the recorded ticket owner (or provided user constrained by _ticketOwner check) and provide no alternate recipient or rescue mechanism. If collateral token policy blocks transfers to that address (blacklist/freeze/compliance lock), claim/refund always reverts. After deadlines, sweeps move leftover market balance to protocolPool, effectively confiscating unclaimable user funds.
trigger_scenario: User commits a ticket and becomes the recorded owner in commitmentUsers[].
Before claiming/refunding, collateral token marks that address as blocked (or otherwise non-receivable).
User (or relayer) attempts claim/refund; _safeTransferExact reverts because token transfer to owner fails.
Ticket remains unclaimed as deadlines continue.
After claim/refund window closes, factory executes sweepUnclaimed or sweepCancelledRefunds.
Remaining balance, including the blocked user's entitlement, is transferred to protocolPool.
preconditions: Collateral token can block/freeze transfers for specific recipient addresses.
Affected ticket owner is blocked before successful claim/refund.

title: Verifier.setVerifyingKey: G2 coordinate order is not canonicalized on-chain so a structurally valid but semantically wrong VK can be installed and brick verification
root_cause: _buildG2 stores beta/gamma/delta FQ2 limbs exactly as provided and _setVerifyingKey only checks non-infinity plus precompile acceptance. There is no canonicalization or on-chain recomputation against a pinned expected key hash at rotation time, so alternate serialization conventions (e.g., unswapped c0/c1 limbs) can pass curve-validity checks while representing a different verifying key.
trigger_scenario: Owner rotates the verifier key using raw vk JSON coordinates from a tool that uses a different FQ2 limb order than the contract expects.
setVerifyingKey calls _buildG2 and accepts the coordinates as-is.
Pairing.isValidG2Point returns success because the swapped point is still a valid curve point.
The contract updates _vk and emits VerifyingKeyUpdated, so governance believes rotation succeeded.
Subsequent valid Groth16 proofs generated for the intended circuit fail in verifyProof because on-chain vk no longer matches the circuit semantics.
Settlement paths that depend on this verifier revert/fail, effectively freezing proof-based finalization until another key rotation occurs.
preconditions: Key rotation is executed through tooling or manual input that does not enforce the verifier's exact FQ2 encoding convention.
The supplied coordinates remain curve-valid, so structural checks do not fail fast.

title: Verifier.setVerifyingKey: single-step privileged key rotation has no staged activation, enabling immediate protocol-wide settlement freeze on shared verifier instances
root_cause: setVerifyingKey performs an immediate in-place replacement of _vk, _ic, circuitHash, and verifyingKeyHash in one owner transaction with no timelock, grace period, dual-approval, or staged next-key activation. Any mistake or compromised owner action instantly mutates the verifier anchor for every consumer using the same verifier address.
trigger_scenario: Multiple active markets rely on one Verifier address and have operational assumptions tied to the current verifyingKeyHash.
Owner key is compromised, or owner executes an incorrect/untimely rotation.
Attacker/operator calls setVerifyingKey with new key material.
verifyingKeyHash and circuitHash change atomically in the same transaction.
Downstream settlement calls that require the previous key anchor fail immediately after rotation.
Markets cannot finalize until governance performs additional recovery actions, creating a liveness outage window.
preconditions: Verifier ownership is a single high-privilege trust boundary without enforced timelock/multisig in this contract.
The verifier contract is shared by active markets that depend on stable key identity.

title: Verifier.verifyProof: bool-return API is fail-hard for malformed proofs because decode and curve validation reverts are outside the catch boundary
root_cause: verifyProof only wraps this._pairingCheck(...) in try/catch. Earlier stages (_decodeProof, _buildG1/_buildG2, _validateG1Point, _validateG2Point) revert on malformed calldata or invalid points via InvalidProofEncoding/FieldOverflow/InvalidCurvePoint, so invalid proofs do not uniformly return false despite the interface's bool semantics.
trigger_scenario: A relayer or integrator accepts proof payloads from an untrusted source and calls verifyProof via a state-changing workflow.
Attacker submits proof bytes with malformed encoding length or off-curve coordinates.
verifyProof hits _decodeProof or _validateG*Point and reverts before entering the try/catch around _pairingCheck.
The parent transaction bubbles the revert instead of receiving a simple false result.
If the parent batches multiple proofs in one transaction, one malformed element aborts the entire batch execution.
An attacker can repeatedly inject malformed payloads to create operational griefing for automated submitters that expect soft-fail boolean behavior.
preconditions: Upstream workflow treats verifyProof as a non-reverting boolean filter and does not pre-simulate malformed payloads.
Proof submissions can be influenced by adversarial actors.

title: Pairing.isValidG2Point: verifier soundness is delegated entirely to precompile success semantics, so non-compliant BN254 implementations can silently weaken validation
root_cause: G2 validation and final proof checking rely on bn254 precompiles (0x08) as the sole correctness oracle. isValidG2Point accepts any input where staticcall succeeds and performs no independent subgroup/consistency checks in Solidity. If a chain/client implementation deviates from EIP-197 failure behavior, malformed twist points can be accepted.
trigger_scenario: Protocol deploys to an environment where bn254 precompile behavior is non-standard or buggy (e.g., missing strict subgroup checks).
Attacker provides malformed G2 data that should be rejected under canonical EIP-197 rules.
Pairing.isValidG2Point returns true because staticcall reports success on that environment.
Verifier accepts malformed key material during rotation or malformed proof points during verification.
pairing checks can then evaluate over invalid group elements, breaking Groth16 soundness assumptions.
Attacker may produce false-positive proof acceptance or induce systemic verification failure depending on the exact precompile deviation.
preconditions: Deployment target does not enforce canonical bn254 precompile validity checks.
Attacker can submit crafted proof/key material to the verifier workflow.

title: Pairing precompile wrappers forward gas() with fail-revert semantics, enabling high-cost griefing when automated submitters relay attacker-controlled malformed proofs
root_cause: Pairing.add/scalarMul/pairing forward all remaining gas into precompile staticcalls and use require(success, ...). On failure paths, large gas chunks can be consumed before reverting, and Verifier only soft-catches the final _pairingCheck call. There is no on-chain gas cap or cheap pre-screening path for untrusted off-chain proof submissions.
trigger_scenario: An attacker feeds malformed proof payloads into a keeper/relayer pipeline that auto-submits settlement transactions.
The relayer submits transactions calling workflows that reach Verifier.verifyProof.
Precompile calls in Pairing consume substantial gas on failing validations/pairing operations.
The transaction reverts or returns false only after expensive cryptographic calls have run.
Attacker repeats submissions with varied malformed payloads.
Keeper operating budget is drained and settlement liveness degrades due repeated high-cost failures.
preconditions: An automated submitter relays proofs from untrusted sources without strict off-chain simulation/validation.
Adversary can continuously supply malformed proof attempts.
